title: Asthma: acute severity, emergency treatment and long-term control
blurb: Grade an acute asthma attack in a child as moderate, acute severe or life-threatening, give first-line treatment, and support long-term control under NICE NG245.
question: Leo, 4, attends the children's emergency department with an asthma attack. He can say only two or three words at a time, his SpO2 is 91% in air and his heart rate is 150. How severe is this attack?

teach.body: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways with variable airflow obstruction, causing wheeze, cough, breathlessness and chest tightness. An acute attack is a worsening that needs extra treatment. In the UK, acute asthma in children is managed using SIGN 158 content within the BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway, and long-term care follows NICE NG245 (2024). Plain English: grade the attack quickly, give reliever and steroids early, and then fix the long-term plan.

values: Cannot complete sentences, or too breathless to feed

teach.caption: Use the worst feature present to grade the attack.

teach.caption: Give early in the attack. A course of up to 3 days is usually enough.

teach.text: A quiet chest is not always good news. A child who becomes quieter while still working hard, tiring or confused may have a silent chest: so little air is moving that wheeze disappears. This is life-threatening and needs immediate senior help.

teach.body: For children aged 5 to 11 with newly diagnosed asthma, offer twice-daily paediatric low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) with a SABA as needed. If not controlled, consider paediatric low-dose MART if the child can manage it. For under-5s with suspected asthma, consider an 8 to 12 week ICS trial. Check inhaler technique and adherence, prescribe a spacer with a metered dose inhaler, and give a personalised asthma action plan.

teach.h: Scenario: Ben, 7, in the emergency department
teach.body: Ben is talking in sentences. SpO2 is 95% in air, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 28. Nurse Ola grades this as moderate: no acute severe features for a child over 5. She gives salbutamol via spacer, one puff at a time with 5 breaths, and oral prednisolone 30 to 40 mg as prescribed, then reassesses. Before discharge she checks Ben's inhaler technique and updates his written action plan with his parents.

items: Use the reliever via spacer at the first sign of an attack.
Seek urgent help if 10 puffs are not controlling symptoms.
Take the preventer every day, even when well.
Know the action plan and bring the inhaler to every review.
Schools can hold a spare emergency reliever inhaler.
Acute severe: cannot complete sentences, SpO2 under 92%, PEF 33–50%, HR over 140 (1–5) / 125 (over 5), RR over 40 / 30.
Life-threatening: SpO2 under 92% plus silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, hypotension, exhaustion, confusion or PEF under 33%.
Salbutamol via spacer first line; nebulised oxygen-driven if SpO2 under 92%; add ipratropium if poor response.
Prednisolone early: 10 mg under 2, 20 mg 2–5, 30–40 mg over 5.
NG245: paediatric low-dose ICS plus SABA as needed for 5–11s; MART next if able.

summary: You can now grade an acute asthma attack in a child, give oxygen, salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisolone appropriately, and recognise a silent chest. You can also support long-term control with NG245 treatment, inhaler technique and an action plan.

A.q: Leo, 4, has an asthma attack. He can say only two or three words at a time, his SpO2 is 91% in air and heart rate is 150. How severe is this attack?
A.why: Unable to complete sentences, SpO2 under 92% and HR over 140 at 1 to 5 years are acute severe features. No life-threatening signs are described.

whyNot.0: Moderate attacks allow talking in sentences with SpO2 92% or more.
whyNot.1: These features are far beyond a mild attack.
whyNot.2: Life-threatening needs SpO2 under 92% plus a feature such as silent chest, cyanosis or exhaustion.

A.q: Zara, 2, has a mild wheezy episode and is prescribed salbutamol by metered dose inhaler. How should it be given?
options: Via a spacer with a face mask
Via a spacer with a mouthpiece
A.why: Salbutamol via pMDI and spacer is first line, and children under 3 need a face mask on the spacer.

whyNot.1: A young child cannot coordinate a pMDI without a spacer.
whyNot.2: A mouthpiece needs a seal she is too young to make; a face mask is used under 3.
whyNot.3: pMDI with spacer is as effective as a nebuliser for mild to moderate attacks.

A.q: Ayaan, 4, is treated for an acute asthma attack. What oral prednisolone dose is appropriate?
A.why: Children aged 2 to 5 years receive 20 mg of oral prednisolone.

whyNot.0: 10 mg is the dose for under 2 years.
whyNot.1: 30 mg is within the over-5 range.
whyNot.3: 40 mg is the upper over-5 dose.

B.q: Grace, 8, has an asthma attack on the ward. She is drowsy, her chest is silent on auscultation and SpO2 is 88% in air. What is the grade and immediate priority?
options: Acute severe; oral prednisolone given first
B.why: SpO2 under 92% with a silent chest and drowsiness is life-threatening. Call senior help, give high-flow oxygen and nebulised bronchodilators.

whyNot.0: A silent chest and drowsiness lift this to life-threatening.
whyNot.1: These are not moderate features, and waiting an hour is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Steroids are given early but do not come before oxygen and bronchodilators.

B.q: Ivy, 6, has had 10 puffs of salbutamol via spacer. Twenty minutes later her SpO2 is 90% in air. What should be given next?
options: Oral salbutamol syrup at a weight-based dose
B.why: If SpO2 is under 92%, give nebulised salbutamol driven by oxygen (2.5 to 5 mg), adding ipratropium if the response is poor.

whyNot.0: With SpO2 under 92%, oxygen-driven nebulised therapy is indicated.
whyNot.2: Oral salbutamol has no role in acute asthma.
whyNot.3: Montelukast is a preventer, not an acute rescue treatment.

B.q: Ben, 7, has a moderate asthma attack. He talks in sentences, SpO2 is 95%, heart rate 118 and respiratory rate 28. Which finding would change his grade to acute severe?
B.why: In children over 5, a heart rate over 125 is an acute severe feature.

whyNot.0: Acute severe in over-5s is RR over 30; 30 is not over.
whyNot.1: 120 is below the over-5 acute severe threshold of 125.
whyNot.2: SpO2 of 93% is still 92% or more.

C.q: Finley, 8, has newly diagnosed asthma. What initial maintenance treatment does NICE NG245 recommend?
options: SABA as needed, with no regular preventer
Low-dose ICS twice daily, SABA as needed
C.why: NG245 rec 1.8.1: twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS with a SABA as needed for 5 to 11-year-olds with newly diagnosed asthma.

whyNot.0: SABA without a preventer is not recommended in NG245.
whyNot.2: An LTRA is considered later if asthma is uncontrolled and MART is unsuitable.
whyNot.3: MART is considered if not controlled on low-dose ICS, starting at low dose.

C.q: Freya, 3, has had two hospital admissions with wheeze and interval symptoms with eczema. Asthma is suspected. What does NG245 suggest?
C.why: NG245 rec 1.9.1: consider an 8 to 12 week trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS in under-5s with suspected asthma and features suggesting maintenance therapy is needed.

whyNot.1: Treatment is not delayed until age 5 when symptoms warrant it.
whyNot.2: Regular oral steroids are not maintenance treatment for asthma.
whyNot.3: LTRA is not the first-line maintenance option in NG245.

C.q: Before discharge after an asthma attack, Ben's mother asks when she should get urgent help next time. What should the nurse say?
options: When he has used his preventer twice
If 4 puffs of reliever have not helped
If 10 puffs of reliever are not helping
When the wheeze has lasted more than 24 hours
C.why: Parents should seek urgent help if 10 puffs of the reliever via spacer are not controlling symptoms.

whyNot.0: The preventer is not used to treat an attack.
whyNot.1: Up to 10 puffs can be given before this threshold.
whyNot.3: Waiting 24 hours with uncontrolled wheeze is unsafe.

reteach.title: Words, sats, effort
reteach.question: What three quick checks tell you how bad a child's asthma attack is?

blocks.body: Can the child talk in sentences? What is the SpO2 in air? How hard are they working, and is air moving? Sentences with SpO2 92% or more is moderate. Broken sentences, SpO2 under 92% or high HR and RR for age is acute severe. Add silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion or confusion and it is life-threatening.

blocks.text: Thresholds change at age 5: HR over 140 and RR over 40 for 1–5 years, but HR over 125 and RR over 30 for over-5s.

explain.body: Moderate: sentences, SpO2 92%+, PEF 50%+. Acute severe: cannot complete sentences, SpO2 under 92%, PEF 33–50%, high HR and RR. Life-threatening: SpO2 under 92% plus silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, hypotension, exhaustion, confusion or PEF under 33%.

test.q: Which is a life-threatening feature of acute asthma in a child?
test.why: Cyanosis with SpO2 under 92% is a life-threatening feature.

whyNot.0: Wheeze is present in all grades.
whyNot.3: RR over 30 in over-5s is acute severe, not life-threatening.

explain.body: Salbutamol via pMDI and spacer: 1 puff at a time with 5 tidal breaths, up to 10 puffs. Face mask under 3. Nebulised oxygen-driven salbutamol if SpO2 under 92%. Add ipratropium 250 micrograms if poor response.

test.q: How should each puff of salbutamol be given via a spacer?
options: One puff, then hold breath 30 s
Two puffs, then one deep breath
test.why: Give one puff at a time into the spacer, followed by 5 tidal breaths.

whyNot.0: Multiple puffs at once reduce the dose delivered.
whyNot.2: Tidal breathing is used with a spacer in children, not a 30-second hold.
whyNot.3: Puffs are given one at a time with tidal breathing.

explain.body: Oral prednisolone early: 10 mg under 2 years, 20 mg 2 to 5 years, 30 to 40 mg over 5 years; usually up to 3 days.

test.q: Lola, 18 months, has an acute wheezy episode treated as asthma. What prednisolone dose is appropriate?

whyNot.0: 20 mg is the 2 to 5 years dose.
whyNot.2: 5 mg is below the recommended dose.

explain.body: NG245: 5 to 11 years start with twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS plus SABA as needed; consider low-dose MART if uncontrolled. Under 5: 8 to 12 week ICS trial if suspected asthma needs maintenance. Spacer, technique checks, action plan.

test.q: Sofia, 9, is uncontrolled on paediatric low-dose ICS plus SABA as needed and can manage a MART regimen. What should be considered?
test.why: NG245 rec 1.8.2: consider paediatric low-dose MART if not controlled on low-dose ICS plus SABA, if the child can manage it.

whyNot.2: Oral salbutamol is not part of the pathway.
whyNot.3: Steps are gradual; high-dose ICS is not the next step.
